difficultyReason: Short, sharply opposed positions on a single topic. Speakers use clear language and directly contradict on whether video games have educational value.
stimulus: Dr. Chen: Video games are primarily entertainment products, and their educational value is incidental. Schools should focus resources on proven teaching methods rather than adopting games in classrooms. Dr. Okonkwo: You underestimate games' potential. Research shows they develop problem-solving skills and engagement. Schools should explore games as educational tools.
questionStem: Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo disagree over whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: video games can develop certain cognitive skills

choices.label: B
choices.text: schools currently use traditional teaching methods

choices.label: C
choices.text: video games should play a role in schools' educational approach

choices.label: D
choices.text: entertainment products lack any value to society

choices.label: E
choices.text: problem-solving is an important skill for students

explanations.correct: Chen denies schools should adopt games; Okonkwo affirms schools should explore games as tools. This is a direct disagreement on whether games should play a role in schools' educational approach.
explanations.A: Both speakers implicitly accept that games can develop skills. Chen concedes educational value; Okonkwo asserts it. This is agreement, not disagreement.
explanations.B: Neither speaker clearly takes a position on this factual claim about current practice.
explanations.C: Correct. Chen opposes schools exploring games; Okonkwo advocates for it.
explanations.D: Neither speaker makes or denies a claim about entertainment products lacking value.
explanations.E: Both speakers would likely agree problem-solving is important. This is not a point of disagreement.

difficultyReason: Two speakers with plainly opposing views on a single clear issue. No shared assumptions; the disagreement is transparent and vocabulary is straightforward.
stimulus: Moreno: Preserving wilderness areas is a luxury we cannot afford. As populations grow, we must convert natural land to housing and agriculture to meet human needs. Peña: That reasoning ignores ecological costs. Destroyed ecosystems cannot be restored, and their loss threatens the survival of countless species and human well-being alike. We must prioritize preservation.
questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: human population is increasing in many regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: ecosystems can recover once damaged

choices.label: C
choices.text: preservation of wilderness should take priority over immediate human needs

choices.label: D
choices.text: species extinction has occurred

choices.label: E
choices.text: housing and agriculture are necessary for human survival

explanations.correct: Moreno prioritizes development for human needs; Peña prioritizes preservation. They directly disagree on whether preservation should take priority over immediate human demands.
explanations.A: Moreno asserts this; Peña does not dispute it. One-sided claim.
explanations.B: Peña denies this; Moreno does not address it explicitly. One-sided.
explanations.C: Correct. Moreno says preservation is a luxury we cannot afford (denies priority); Peña says we must prioritize preservation (affirms priority).
explanations.D: Neither speaker disputes that extinction occurs; this is background fact.
explanations.E: Both speakers appear to accept this. No disagreement.

difficultyReason: Clear dialogue with opposing stances on a single axis. Speakers have distinct and incompatible positions on the merits of a proposal.
stimulus: Laird: Remote work policies undermine team cohesion and company culture. Employees need in-person collaboration to build trust and share knowledge effectively. Kim: You ignore the data. Studies show remote workers are equally productive and less stressed. Companies should embrace flexibility because it benefits employees without sacrificing output.
questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: remote work reduces employee stress levels

choices.label: B
choices.text: company culture is important for business success

choices.label: C
choices.text: remote work arrangements should be a standard company policy

choices.label: D
choices.text: employees value workplace flexibility

choices.label: E
choices.text: in-person collaboration enables knowledge sharing

explanations.correct: Laird opposes remote work policies, saying they harm culture; Kim advocates for them. They disagree on whether remote work should be standard policy.
explanations.A: Kim affirms this; Laird does not explicitly deny it. One-sided.
explanations.B: Both speakers seem to accept this. Not a disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct. Laird rejects remote work policies; Kim says companies should embrace them.
explanations.D: Both speakers could accept this. Not a clear disagreement.
explanations.E: Laird affirms this; Kim does not directly deny it. One-sided.

difficultyReason: Straightforward dialogue with opposing positions on a concrete topic. The disagreement is explicit and unmistakable.
stimulus: Dr. Okonkwo: Mandatory standardized testing in schools wastes instructional time and narrows curriculum. It measures only a limited set of skills and has not improved student learning outcomes. Schools should eliminate these tests. Dr. Chen: Testing provides essential accountability data. Without standardized measures, schools cannot identify which students need help or compare performance across districts. Testing must continue.
questionStem: Dr. Okonkwo and Dr. Chen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: standardized testing measures a wide range of student skills

choices.label: B
choices.text: some students struggle academically

choices.label: C
choices.text: schools should retain standardized testing requirements

choices.label: D
choices.text: accountability in education serves a purpose

choices.label: E
choices.text: testing narrows what subjects are taught in schools

explanations.correct: Dr. Okonkwo argues schools should eliminate tests; Dr. Chen argues they must continue. They directly disagree on whether tests should be retained.
explanations.A: Dr. Okonkwo denies this; Dr. Chen does not address it. One-sided.
explanations.B: Neither speaker disputes this premise. Both would likely agree.
explanations.C: Correct. Okonkwo opposes retention; Chen supports it.
explanations.D: Both speakers recognize accountability has some value. Not a disagreement.
explanations.E: Okonkwo asserts this; Chen does not directly deny it. One-sided.

difficultyReason: Simple, opposed statements on a single issue. Speakers reach directly contradictory conclusions about the same topic.
stimulus: Peña: Artificial intelligence should be designed to mimic human judgment as closely as possible. If AI systems cannot explain their decisions the way humans do, they are unreliable and unsafe for critical applications. Moreno: That expectation is misguided. AI does not need to think like humans to be effective. AI systems can be reliable even if they operate through processes we do not fully understand. The focus should be on verifiable outcomes, not on replicating human reasoning.
questionStem: Peña and Moreno disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: artificial intelligence has been deployed in critical applications

choices.label: B
choices.text: AI systems that operate through processes humans do not understand can still be reliable

choices.label: C
choices.text: human judgment is a valuable decision-making approach

choices.label: D
choices.text: verifiable outcomes are important for assessing AI performance

choices.label: E
choices.text: AI should be easier for humans to understand

explanations.correct: Peña denies that AI with unexplainable processes is reliable; Moreno affirms that such systems can be reliable. Direct disagreement on whether AI can be reliable without human-like reasoning.
explanations.A: Neither speaker clearly disputes this factual claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Peña says unexplainable AI is unreliable; Moreno says it can be reliable.
explanations.C: Both speakers implicitly accept human judgment has value. No disagreement.
explanations.D: Moreno affirms this; Peña does not deny it. One-sided.
explanations.E: Moreno does not address whether AI should be easier to understand. One-sided.

difficultyReason: Direct opposition on a central topic with clear supporting reasoning. The speakers reach opposite conclusions about a simple factual and evaluative question.
stimulus: Laird: The historical novel is a legitimate form of serious literature. Blending historical facts with imaginative narrative allows authors to explore human experience in ways pure history cannot. This hybrid approach enriches understanding. Kim: Historical novels mislead readers. By mixing fact and fiction without clear boundaries, they obscure what actually happened. Readers should study history through factual sources, not novels.
questionStem: Laird and Kim disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: historical novels contain some factual elements

choices.label: B
choices.text: understanding human experience is valuable

choices.label: C
choices.text: historical novels should be considered a serious literary form

choices.label: D
choices.text: factual sources exist about historical events

choices.label: E
choices.text: authors sometimes incorporate imagination into their work

explanations.correct: Laird affirms the historical novel is a legitimate serious literary form; Kim denies it, recommending readers avoid novels in favor of factual sources. They disagree on whether novels deserve recognition as serious literature.
explanations.A: Both speakers implicitly accept that novels contain historical facts. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Both speakers would accept this. Not a point of disagreement.
explanations.C: Correct. Laird endorses novels as serious literature; Kim rejects them as such.
explanations.D: Both speakers acknowledge factual historical sources exist. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers recognize authors use imagination. No disagreement.

difficultyReason: Clear, opposing proposals with distinct reasoning. Speakers take unambiguous positions on the same evaluative question.
stimulus: Dr. Chen: Patent laws should protect pharmaceutical innovations for longer periods to incentivize drug development. The high cost of research justifies extended monopolies that let companies recoup investments. Dr. Okonkwo: Longer patents delay generic competition and keep life-saving drugs unaffordable for most patients. Access to medicine matters more than pharmaceutical profits. Patents should be shorter to speed generic availability.
questionStem: Dr. Chen and Dr. Okonkwo disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: developing new pharmaceuticals requires significant financial investment

choices.label: B
choices.text: generic drugs are less effective than brand-name drugs

choices.label: C
choices.text: patent protections should be extended to incentivize pharmaceutical innovation

choices.label: D
choices.text: access to medicine is important

choices.label: E
choices.text: pharmaceutical companies have costs they must recover

explanations.correct: Dr. Chen advocates for longer patents to incentivize innovation; Dr. Okonkwo opposes extended patents because they restrict access. They disagree on whether patent protections should be extended.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept this. Dr. Chen uses it as justification; Dr. Okonkwo does not dispute it. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Neither speaker claims this. Not addressed.
explanations.C: Correct. Chen supports extension; Okonkwo opposes it.
explanations.D: Both speakers clearly accept this. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers implicitly recognize this. No disagreement.

difficultyReason: Opposing evaluations of a single proposal. Speakers differ sharply on whether a policy is warranted, with clear supporting statements.
stimulus: Moreno: Public funding for museums is wasteful. Museums serve only affluent patrons who can afford to visit. Governments should redirect resources to essential services like healthcare and schools. Peña: Museums educate the entire community and preserve cultural heritage that belongs to everyone. Subsidized admission allows poor families to access culture. Public funding for museums is a worthwhile investment in social well-being.
questionStem: Moreno and Peña disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: museums have visitors from different economic backgrounds

choices.label: B
choices.text: government resources are limited

choices.label: C
choices.text: public funding of museums is a justified expenditure

choices.label: D
choices.text: cultural heritage has value

choices.label: E
choices.text: healthcare and education are important public services

explanations.correct: Moreno calls public museum funding wasteful; Peña calls it a worthwhile investment. They disagree on whether public funding of museums is justified.
explanations.A: Moreno asserts museums serve mainly the affluent; Peña implies subsidized access helps poor families. However, the core disagreement is not about current visitor composition but about whether funding is justified.
explanations.B: Neither speaker disputes this. Both accept it implicitly.
explanations.C: Correct. Moreno opposes the expenditure; Peña supports it as worthwhile.
explanations.D: Peña asserts this; Moreno does not deny it. One-sided.
explanations.E: Both speakers likely accept this. No disagreement.

difficultyReason: Plainly opposed positions on a single question. Speakers use straightforward language and reach directly contradictory conclusions.
stimulus: Dr. Okonkwo: Bilingual education programs are essential. They allow non-English-speaking students to learn academic content while developing English proficiency. Students educated bilingually perform better academically than those in English-only classrooms. Dr. Chen: Immersion in English is faster and more efficient. Bilingual programs dilute instruction and slow English acquisition. Students benefit more from intensive English instruction without the distraction of a second language.
questionStem: Dr. Okonkwo and Dr. Chen disagree about whether

choices.label: A
choices.text: English language proficiency is important for students

choices.label: B
choices.text: bilingual education programs improve academic performance compared to English-only approaches

choices.label: C
choices.text: non-English-speaking students exist in schools

choices.label: D
choices.text: some instructional approaches are more efficient than others

choices.label: E
choices.text: students can learn multiple languages simultaneously

explanations.correct: Dr. Okonkwo affirms that bilingual students perform better academically; Dr. Chen denies this, claiming English-only immersion is more effective. They directly disagree on the comparative academic outcomes.
explanations.A: Both speakers accept English proficiency is important. No disagreement.
explanations.B: Correct. Okonkwo claims bilingual students perform better; Chen claims English-only is more effective.
explanations.C: Both speakers acknowledge these students exist. No disagreement.
explanations.D: Both speakers implicitly accept this general principle. No disagreement.
explanations.E: Both speakers implicitly accept this is possible. No disagreement.
